title: Eluned Morgan, Vaughan Gething, and the £200k donation scandal
narrative_md:
**Vaughan Gething lasted 136 days as First Minister — the shortest tenure in the history of devolved Wales.**

On 16 March 2024 Vaughan Gething became Wales's first Black First Minister. On 5 June he lost a vote of no confidence. On 16 July he resigned. The cause: a £200,000 donation to his Labour leadership campaign from a businessman whose company had received £400,000 in COVID-era loans from a Welsh Government-owned bank.

The donor was David Neal, owner of Dauson Environmental Group, which had received two loans totalling roughly £400,000 from the Development Bank of Wales — a Welsh Government ALB — between 2020 and 2022. Neal had previously been convicted of environmental offences. His donations to Gething's leadership campaign, split into two tranches of £100,000 and £100,000 in late 2023, were the largest individual donations in Welsh Labour's history.

Gething denied any conflict of interest, pointing out that DBW loan decisions were operationally independent. But the optics were fatal in a devolved polity that prides itself on small-scale accountability. Opposition parties — Plaid Cymru, Welsh Conservatives and Lib Dems — demanded his resignation; Welsh Labour backbenchers Lee Waters, Hannah Blythyn (whom Gething sacked during the crisis) and Jenny Rathbone broke publicly with the leadership.

The confidence vote on 5 June 2024 passed 29-27 on cross-party lines. It was not constitutionally binding — unlike at Westminster, the Senedd's confidence procedure is symbolic — but politically it was unsurvivable. Gething attempted a reshuffle, then a pause, then on 16 July announced his resignation. The leadership contest that followed was short and decisive.

Eluned Morgan was elected unopposed on 6 August 2024 — the first woman First Minister of Wales and a former MEP, peer, and health minister. She inherited a government with a £354 million in-year budget pressure, the Betsi Cadwaladr health board crisis, and an upcoming Senedd expansion from 60 to 96 members under the Senedd Cymru (Members and Elections) Act 2024, legislated in June 2024 and taking effect from the May 2026 election.

The 96-member Senedd is the most significant constitutional change in Welsh devolution since 2011. Elections will use a closed-list proportional system across 16 new constituencies, each returning six members. Critics argue the reform was rushed through during a crisis in Labour's Welsh leadership; supporters argue the current 60-seat chamber is too small to scrutinise a government with a £25 billion budget.

The Gething episode is the first genuine Welsh political scandal of the devolved era. Comparison with Scottish events is informative: Nicola Sturgeon's 2023 resignation over a separate police investigation, Humza Yousaf's 2024 collapse over the Bute House Agreement, and Gething's fall all occurred within 15 months. Devolution now has the same pace of leadership turnover as Westminster.

Financially, Welsh Government funding continues to flow through the Barnett formula: £21 billion in Welsh Block Grant 2024-25, supplemented by the Wales Reserve. The Wales Office — the UK Government department that administers the relationship — was kept, despite 2024 manifesto suggestions it might be folded into a single Territorial Office.

Morgan faces the 2026 election as the first incumbent to lead the new 96-member Senedd. Early polling suggests Welsh Labour will be the largest party but short of a majority — meaning Wales is heading towards its first formal coalition since 2007-11.
